To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the sickle cell trait is associated, in children, with controlled levels of hem and mild pro-inflammatory response during acute malaria.

the HbAS hemoglobin variant is associated with controlled haem levels, reduced induction of haem oxygenase‐1 (an enzyme that catabolyzes haem) and mild proinflammatoy response during malaria infection.

Sickle cell trait, a genetic variant of haemoglobin (Hb) that is prevalent in sub-Saharan Africa, is associated with controlled concentrations of haem and reduced induction of haem catabolizing enzyme, haem oxygenase‐1, during acute malaria infection, compared to Hb normal (HbAA) genotype.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the role of the HbAS hemoglobin genotype in the regulation of haem metabolism during malaria infection, which is an important step towards understanding the mechanism by which this genotype confers resistance to severe malaria.
understanding the mechanism by which HbAS genotype protects against severe malaria.
the role of the sickle cell trait in the control of haematological pathologies associated with malaria infection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the controlled induction of HO‐I during acute P. falciparum infection is associated with the HbAS phenotype and is linked to reduced susceptibility to severe pathologies of malaria.
the HbAS phenotype is associated with a reduced accumulation of haem, controlled levels of HO-1 and milder inflammatory responses during acute malaria infection compared with Hb AA.
HbAS genotype confers reduced susceptibility of severe malaria by controlling haem and inducing HO‐1, leading to milder proinflammation responses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
sickle cell trait (HbAS) may be a mechanism of protection against severe malaria by controlling the accumulation of toxic haem, and the subsequent proinflammatory responses.

the controlled levels of haematopoiesis, haem and HO‐1 during acute malaria in children with the HbAS phenotype, may be a contributing factor in the reduced susceptibility of this genotype to severe malaria pathophysiology.
the controlled induction of HO‐ 1 in HbAS may be responsible for the reduced susceptibility of HbAS to malaria complications.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the HbAS sickle cell trait may confer protection against severe malaria pathologies through the control of haematological parameters and proinflammatory responses.
HbAS genotype is associated with controlled haem accumulation during acute malaria, leading to a milder proinflamatory response.

the HbAS hemoglobin genotype confers protection to severe malaria by a mechanism which involves controlled induction of the haem catabolic enzyme, haemoxygenase-1, and relatively milder proinflamatory responses during acute malaria infection.
